messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Roofer
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells
  Maladaptive Strategies: Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Avoid Assertiveness: never disagree or assert myself to avoid conflict, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Hopelessness: I have no future, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Boun had spent forty years as a roofer, his body attuned to the sun and the specific balance required to move across a steep pitch. At sixty-six, he was still strong, the man his family relied on. That changed eight months ago, on a hot afternoon re-sealing the roof of a small manufacturing plant. A pressure valve on an exhaust stack released with a violent hiss, bathing him in a plume of acrid, invisible chemicals. The world tilted, his lungs burned, and he remembers a frantic scramble away from the vent before his vision narrowed and the paramedics were looking down at him. The next clear memory was the sterile, antiseptic smell of the hospital, a scent that now clung to him like a shroud.

In the first few weeks home, the event replayed itself relentlessly. It wasn't just a memory; it was a film, vivid and detailed, that would start without warning—the hiss of the valve, the dizzying view of the ground, the burning in his chest. When these memories ambushed him, Boun would retreat into himself, trying desperately to push the images away while simultaneously dwelling on the man he used to be before the accident, a man who wasn't afraid of the sky. Sometimes, even more unsettlingly, the terror would arrive without a picture; he would be sitting at the dinner table and suddenly feel the full, suffocating emotional intensity of the event, his heart hammering for a reason his mind couldn't see.

Soon, the world began to fill with invisible tripwires. The sharp smell of his wife’s cleaning ammonia would send him reeling back to the rooftop, sparking the memory reel and an immediate, frantic effort to suppress it. A routine doctor’s visit became an ordeal; the hospital smell in the waiting room was enough to make him feel profoundly unsafe, a suffocating sense that danger was imminent and he was unable to relax. This pervasive sense of threat began to bleed into everything. When he felt this agitated and on edge, he found the vivid memories of the accident were even more likely to break through his defenses. To manage the feeling, he started avoiding any place he didn't know, turning down his son’s invitations to new restaurants because he couldn’t assess the danger in an unfamiliar layout.

This retreat inward solidified into a devastating cycle. Waking up in the pitch-black of night became a recurring terror. The darkness itself was a trigger, plunging him into a state of high alert that made sleep impossible. He would lie there, rigid and unable to relax, convinced that some unseen threat was gathering. To cope, he would try to force the thoughts from his mind, a strategy that only made him feel weaker when it failed. This failure fed a growing, painful belief: he couldn't rely on himself anymore. This appraisal, that he was fundamentally broken and untrustworthy, became the lens through which he saw everything. It amplified his sense of ambient threat, making the world outside his home feel impossibly dangerous. His belief that danger was everywhere seemed to make him even more sensitive to the faintest chemical scent.

The more he saw the world as a dangerous place, the more he clung to his strategies of avoidance and suppression. He stopped disagreeing with his wife, even on small things, desperate to avoid any conflict that might tax his frayed nerves. He spent hours sitting silently, dwelling on his past strength, a habit that only highlighted his current feelings of hopelessness. Each time he tried and failed to suppress a memory, it was fresh evidence for his most painful conclusion: "I am not the man I was." The memory of his own helplessness on that roof directly fueled his appraisal that he was no longer capable. This conviction that he had no future, that he was permanently damaged, made him retreat further, avoiding people and places, which in turn reinforced the feeling that the world was hostile and he was right to fear it. His work, once a source of pride, was now a source of dread; he turned down any job on a commercial building, his income dwindling as his world shrank.

It was after he refused to attend his granddaughter’s fifth birthday party, held at a community hall he’d never been to, that his wife found him crying in the garage. The shame of his own fear was overwhelming. He came to therapy not with a clear hope, but with a desperate question: could he ever feel safe in his own home again, in his own mind? He feels he has no future, but he clings to the small, fading possibility of being a grandfather his family can rely on, even if he no longer believes he can rely on himself.
